"[]"	"[{\"city\":\"Columbia\",\"state\":\"SC\",\"count\":13},{\"city\":\"ARLINGTON\",\"state\":\"VA\",\"count\":7},{\"city\":\"Miami\",\"state\":\"FL\",\"count\":6},{\"city\":\"UPPER\",\"state\":\"\",\"count\":6},{\"city\":\"RANDOLPH\",\"state\":\"MA\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Naples\",\"state\":\"FL\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Houston\",\"state\":\"TX\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Saint\",\"state\":\"\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Columbus\",\"state\":\"OH\",\"count\":5},{\"city\":\"Grand Rapids\",\"state\":\"MI\",\"count\":4}]"	What if I told you that you could make an extra four thousand dollars a month without buying a single property, without having good credit, and without needing a hundred thousand dollars in the bank? I know that sounds like something somebody made up. But I'm about to break down the exact math, dollar for dollar, so you can see for yourself why this actually works.

Stay with me. Because by the end of this, you're going to understand exactly how ordinary people — not real estate moguls, not trust fund babies, just regular people with a plan — are building real income using a strategy called Airbnb arbitrage. And I'm not going to just explain the concept. I'm going to show you the real numbers. The ones most people won't show you because they're too busy selling you a dream. I don't sell dreams. I sell math. And math doesn't lie.

So let me set the scene. Picture this. You and I are sitting across from each other at a coffee shop. You just told me you need to make more money. Maybe you've got a nine to five that covers the basics, but there's nothing left over. Maybe you've been Googling side hustles at two in the morning. Maybe you heard somebody talking about Airbnb and you thought, that sounds nice, but I don't own property, so that's not for me. And I'm sitting here telling you — that's exactly who this is for. You don't need to own anything. You just need to understand how the math works. So let me walk you through it step by step, the same way I'd explain it to my little cousin if she asked me how I make money.
Here's teaching point number one. What Airbnb arbitrage actually is and why the math behind it works every single time.

Arbitrage is a fancy word. But all it means is this — you pay one price for something, and then you charge a higher price for the same thing. That's it. You buy a pack of water bottles for three dollars at Costco and sell each one for a dollar at a baseball game. You paid three dollars. You made ten. The difference is yours. That's arbitrage. Now apply that same idea to an apartment.

You go find a regular apartment. The kind you'd normally just live in. You sign a normal lease. Let's say the rent is twelve hundred dollars a month. Now instead of just living there, you furnish it. You make it look nice. You put it on Airbnb. And now instead of one person paying twelve hundred dollars a month, you've got guests paying you every single night. Short-term guests — travelers, people on work trips, couples on weekend getaways — they're paying a nightly rate that is two to three times higher than what long-term rent costs in the same area. That's not my opinion. That's just how the short-term rental market works. A place that rents for twelve hundred a month as a regular apartment can bring in two thousand, twenty-five hundred, even three thousand a month when you rent it out by the night on Airbnb. The gap between what you pay in rent and what guests pay you — that gap is your money. That's the money you actually keep.

Now let me show you this with real data, not made-up numbers. According to Coach Inayah market data — and this is pulled from actual listings, actual bookings, actual performance — the average one-bedroom property on our platform brings in two thousand and six dollars a month. That's real. Two thousand and six dollars. At what per night? Ninety-eight dollars a night. And how often is it booked? Sixty-seven percent of the time. That means out of thirty nights in a month, that place is booked about twenty of them. Twenty nights times ninety-eight dollars a night. That's how you get to just over two thousand a month in money coming in.

Now here's why that matters. If you're renting that same one-bedroom for, say, a thousand dollars a month — and plenty of markets have one-bedrooms at that price — you're bringing in two thousand and keeping the difference after expenses. That's real profit from a place you don't even own. And I want you to sit with that for a second. Because most people think you need to buy a house to make money in real estate. You don't. You need to understand the math.
Now let me take you to teaching point number two, and I want to tell you a story to make this real.

Let's say there's someone named Maya. Maya lives in Columbia, South Carolina. And I'm using Columbia for a reason — it's the number one most searched city on our platform right now. Thirteen searches in the last cycle alone. People are looking at Columbia because the rent is affordable and the short-term rental demand is real. College town. State capital. Steady flow of visitors year-round.

So Maya finds a two-bedroom apartment in Columbia. Rent is twelve hundred dollars a month. She puts down first month's rent and a security deposit — that's twenty-four hundred. Then she furnishes it. Now here's where people get scared. They think furnishing means spending fifteen thousand dollars at Pottery Barn. No. Maya goes to Facebook Marketplace. She goes to estate sales. She hits up IKEA. She gets a bed, a couch, some dishes, towels, a TV, and some nice-looking decor. She spends about a thousand dollars. Maybe twelve hundred. So her total to get started — deposit, first month, and furniture — is somewhere between three thousand and four thousand dollars. Not twenty thousand. Not fifty thousand. Under four thousand to launch her first unit.

Now she lists it on Airbnb. She charges a hundred and fifty dollars a night. It's a nice two-bedroom. It sleeps four. Couples love it. Small families love it. At sixty-seven percent booking rate — same rate our data shows — she's booked about twenty nights a month. Twenty nights times a hundred fifty a night. That's three thousand dollars in money coming in. Now subtract her rent — twelve hundred. Subtract her operating costs. That's cleaning fees she pays her cleaner, toiletries, laundry supplies, her Wi-Fi bill, her software for managing the listing. Call that another three to four hundred a month. So she's spending roughly sixteen hundred a month total. She's bringing in three thousand. She's keeping about twelve hundred to fourteen hundred dollars in profit. From one apartment.
And she didn't buy anything. She doesn't have a mortgage. She doesn't need a seven hundred credit score. She signed a lease, furnished a space, and listed it. That's the whole business model.
Now let me take you to teaching point number three. This is where we talk about how you actually hit four thousand dollars a month. Because I know that's the number that brought you here.

If one unit makes Maya about twelve hundred to fourteen hundred dollars a month in profit, how does she get to four thousand? She gets a second unit. And then a third. Three units, each making somewhere between twelve hundred and fifteen hundred a month in profit. That's thirty-six hundred to forty-five hundred a month. Right in that four thousand dollar sweet spot.

Now I know what you're thinking. Three apartments? That sounds like a lot. But here's the thing — you don't do all three at once. You start with one. You learn the process. You get your systems down. Your cleaning schedule. Your guest communication. Your pricing strategy. You figure out what works. And then you take the profit from unit one and you use it to launch unit two. The money from the business funds the growth of the business. That's how you scale without going broke.

And let me give you the real numbers on what three units looks like. Three leases at twelve hundred a month — that's thirty-six hundred in rent. Three units bringing in about three thousand each — that's nine thousand in total money coming in. Operating expenses across all three — maybe twelve hundred total. So you're spending forty-eight hundred a month and bringing in nine thousand. That's forty-two hundred in profit. Four thousand two hundred dollars. Every single month. From apartments you don't own.

And this is not some best-case-scenario fantasy. These are based on the actual average numbers our data shows — sixty-seven percent booking rate, ninety-eight dollars a night for one-bedrooms, and higher for two-bedrooms. I'm being conservative with these numbers on purpose. Because I'd rather you be pleasantly surprised than disappointed.

Now let me address the thing that stops most people. Fear. Specifically the fear that this costs too much to start. I hear it all the time. People tell me, Inayah, I don't have twenty thousand dollars. And I say, good, because you don't need twenty thousand dollars. Your first unit can be launched for somewhere between twenty-five hundred and four thousand dollars. That's deposit, first month's rent, and furnishing on a budget. Is it a lot of money? For some people, yes. But compare that to buying a rental property where you need thirty, forty, fifty thousand dollars for a down payment. Compare it to starting a franchise where you need a hundred thousand. This is one of the lowest-cost entry points into real estate that exists. And the returns start coming in within your first month of bookings.

The other fear I hear is — how do I even know if a property will make money before I sign the lease? And that is the most important question you can ask. Because signing a lease on a property that won't perform is how people lose money in this business. You have to run the numbers first. Not guess. Not hope. Not go off what some guy on TikTok said he made last month. You need to look at what similar places nearby are actually making. You need to check the rules in your city to make sure short-term rentals are even allowed. You need to see how often listings in that neighborhood are actually getting booked. And you need a tool that gives you a clear answer — is this deal worth it or not.

That's exactly why I built the free tool at coachinayahturnkeytool.com. And when I say free, I mean free. No credit card. No trial period. No bait and switch. You go to the site, you type in an address or a city, and it shows you exactly what that property could make. It pulls from real market data — actual listings, actual booking rates, actual nightly prices. It checks whether short-term rentals are legal in that city. It finds properties in your target market. It shows you what every competitor nearby is making. And then it gives you a verdict — go, caution, or pass — with a confidence score so you know exactly how strong the deal is. Nine tools in one platform, completely free. People are already using it. Columbia, South Carolina. Arlington, Virginia. Miami, Florida. Randolph, Massachusetts. These are real cities real people are researching right now on the platform.

I built this because when I started, I had to do all of this research manually. It took me hours. Sometimes days. And I still wasn't sure if my numbers were right. I don't want that for you. I want you to be able to sit down, spend fifteen minutes on the tool, and know — with real data — whether a deal is worth pursuing. That's how you make smart decisions. That's how you avoid expensive mistakes. And that's how you build a portfolio that actually hits four thousand a month in profit.

So let me recap everything we just covered. Airbnb arbitrage means you rent a property with a regular lease, furnish it, and list it on Airbnb. Guests pay you by the night at rates that are two to three times higher than what you pay in rent. The difference — after expenses — is the money you actually keep. The average one-bedroom on our platform brings in two thousand and six dollars a month at sixty-seven percent booking rate and ninety-eight dollars a night. One unit can profit twelve hundred to fifteen hundred a month. Three units gets you to four thousand a month. Your startup cost for unit one is between twenty-five hundred and four thousand dollars. And you don't guess whether a deal works — you use data to know before you sign anything.

Here's what I want you to do right now. Go to coachinayahturnkeytool.com. Type in the city you're thinking about. Pick a property. And let the tool show you the real numbers — what it could make, how often it would be booked, and whether it's actually worth it. It's completely free. No sign-up required. Stop guessing and start knowing. The link is in the description. I'll see you in the next one.
